content: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) encompasses a group of disorders that affect the heart and blood vessels. These include coronary artery diseases (CAD) such as angina and myocardial infarction (commonly referred to as heart attacks). Other forms of CVD include stroke, heart failure, hypertensive heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, congenital heart defects, valvular heart disease, myocarditis, aortic aneurysms, peripheral artery disease, thromboembolic disease, and venous thrombosis. The underlying mechanisms of CVD vary depending on the specific condition. For example, coronary artery disease, stroke, and peripheral artery disease are often linked to atherosclerosis, a condition characterized by the buildup of fatty deposits in the arteries. Risk factors for atherosclerosis include high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, physical inactivity, obesity, high cholesterol, poor diet, and excessive alcohol consumption. High blood pressure alone accounts for 13% of CVD-related deaths, while smoking contributes to 9%, diabetes to 6%, physical inactivity to 6%, and obesity to 5%. Rheumatic heart disease, on the other hand, can develop as a complication of untreated streptococcal throat infections. It is estimated that up to 90% of CVD cases are preventable. Prevention strategies focus on addressing modifiable risk factors through healthy eating, regular physical activity, avoiding tobacco use, and limiting alcohol intake. Managing conditions such as hypertension, high cholesterol, and diabetes is also crucial. Treating streptococcal throat infections with antibiotics can reduce the risk of rheumatic heart disease. The role of aspirin in primary prevention for otherwise healthy individuals remains unclear. Globally, cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death, except in Africa. Deaths from CVD have been increasing in many developing countries, while rates have declined in most developed nations since the 1970s. Coronary artery disease and stroke account for the majority of CVD-related deaths, with 80% of deaths in men and 75% in women attributed to these conditions. CVD primarily affects older adults, with prevalence increasing significantly with age. In the United States, 11% of individuals aged 20–40 have CVD, compared to 37% of those aged 40–60, 71% of those aged 60–80, and 85% of those over 80. The average age of death from coronary artery disease is approximately 80 years in developed countries and 68 years in developing countries. Men typically experience disease onset 7–10 years earlier than women. There are numerous types of cardiovascular diseases. Vascular diseases include coronary artery disease (also known as ischemic heart disease), peripheral arterial disease (affecting blood vessels in the arms and legs), cerebrovascular disease (affecting blood vessels in the brain, including stroke), renal artery stenosis, and aortic aneurysms. Cardiac diseases include cardiomyopathy (diseases of the heart muscle), hypertensive heart disease (secondary to high blood pressure), heart failure (inability of the heart to meet the body's metabolic demands), pulmonary heart disease (right-sided heart failure due to lung disease), arrhythmias (abnormal heart rhythms), inflammatory heart diseases such as endocarditis (inflammation of the heart's inner lining, often involving the valves) and myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle), valvular heart disease, congenital heart defects (structural abnormalities present at birth), and rheumatic heart disease (damage to the heart muscle and valves caused by rheumatic fever, a complication of streptococcal infections). Risk factors for cardiovascular diseases include age, gender, tobacco use, physical inactivity, excessive alcohol consumption, unhealthy diet, obesity, genetic predisposition, family history of CVD, high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, psychosocial factors, poverty, low educational status, and air pollution. While some risk factors, such as age, gender, and genetic predisposition, are non-modifiable, many others can be addressed through lifestyle changes, social interventions, and medical treatments. For example, obesity increases the risk of coronary artery atherosclerosis. Genetics play a significant role in the development of CVD, particularly in men under 55 and women under 65. A family history of CVD triples an individual's risk. Although genetic association studies have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) linked to CVD, their individual impact is small, and the overall genetic contributions to CVD remain poorly understood. Age is the most significant risk factor for developing cardiovascular diseases, with the risk tripling with each decade of life. Fatty streaks in coronary arteries can begin forming during adolescence. Approximately 82% of individuals who die from coronary heart disease are aged 65 or older. The risk of stroke doubles every decade after age 55. Aging is associated with increased serum cholesterol levels, reduced arterial elasticity, and structural changes in the vascular wall, all of which contribute to coronary artery disease. Men are at greater risk of heart disease than premenopausal women. After menopause, women's risk increases, potentially due to decreased estrogen levels, which may have protective effects on glucose metabolism, endothelial function, and lipid profiles. Estrogen reduction post-menopause can lead to more atherogenic lipid profiles, with decreased HDL cholesterol and increased LDL and total cholesterol levels. Gender differences in body composition, heart rate, and arterial compliance also contribute to variations in CVD risk. Women are less likely to receive guideline-based treatments during hospitalization compared to men. Certain racial and ethnic groups, including African-Americans, Hispanics, and South Asians, have higher rates of CVD and related mortality. Disparities in access to care and other health inequities contribute to these differences. Black patients are less likely to receive guideline-based treatments compared to white patients. Tobacco use, including exposure to second-hand smoke, accounts for approximately 10% of CVD cases. Quitting smoking by age 30 significantly reduces the risk of death to levels comparable to non-smokers. Physical inactivity is the fourth leading risk factor for global mortality. Regular physical activity reduces the risk of ischemic heart disease and diabetes by nearly one-third and improves weight management, blood glucose control, blood pressure, lipid profiles, and insulin sensitivity. Dietary factors also play a critical role in cardiovascular health. High intake of saturated fats, trans fats, and salt, along with low consumption of fruits, vegetables, and fish, are linked to increased CVD risk. Replacing saturated fats with polyunsaturated fats and reducing trans fat intake can lower cardiovascular risk. Excessive sugar consumption is associated with higher blood pressure, unfavorable lipid profiles, and increased diabetes risk. Processed meats and high dietary salt intake are also linked to higher CVD risk. Alcohol consumption has a complex relationship with CVD, with moderate intake potentially reducing risk, while excessive intake increases it. Socioeconomic disadvantage is a significant determinant of CVD risk, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Policies that exacerbate socioeconomic inequalities are associated with greater disparities in CVD outcomes. Psychosocial factors, environmental exposures, and healthcare access contribute to these differences. Air pollution, particularly long-term exposure to particulate matter (PM2.5), increases the risk of atherosclerosis, inflammation, and cardiovascular mortality. Occupational exposures to toxins, extreme temperatures, and stress are also linked to CVD. Certain workplace exposures, such as silica dust, engine exhaust, and welding fumes, are associated with heart disease and stroke. Atherosclerosis, the primary precursor to CVD, begins in childhood. Early education and prevention measures are essential to reduce the burden of CVD. Obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and hypercholesterolemia are closely linked to CVD. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among individuals with diabetes, who are 2–4 times more likely to die from CVD-related causes than non-diabetics. Screening for CVD involves assessing risk factors such as age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and diabetes. Risk scores, such as the ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations, estimate 10-year CVD risk. Lipid testing in children with a family history of heart disease is recommended starting at age 2. Routine ECG screening is not recommended for asymptomatic individuals at low risk. Biomarkers such as C-reactive protein and NT-proBNP are under evaluation but lack clear evidence for routine use. Preventive measures include smoking cessation, a healthy diet, regular exercise, limiting alcohol intake, managing blood pressure and cholesterol, and reducing body fat. Psychosocial stress reduction may also be beneficial. Combining multiple preventive strategies is recommended, although evidence on their long-term impact on CVD events is limited.
